title: Three vehicles, one path
hook: Tibetans describe practicing all three vehicles together: renunciation, compassion, and the diamond path

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vajrayana: the vajra in one hand, the bell in the other, tantra, ritual and a close bond with a teacher. Your line was the diamond vehicle. When did your hands, voice and attention all land in one thing? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-seven.

A Tibetan monk gets dressed in the morning. The robes he puts on carry the vows of a monk: no killing, no stealing, a simple life. Before breakfast he recites a prayer to wake up for the sake of every living being. Later, in the shrine room, he picks up the vajra and the bell and chants a mantra. Three things in one morning, and to him they aren't three separate religions or even three separate schools. They're three layers of one practice, stacked like the floors of a house. Today: three vehicles, one path.
screen: `A MONK'S MORNING.` → `THREE LAYERS, ONE HOUSE.` → `THREE VEHICLES, ONE PATH.`

segments.voice: First, the word vehicle. In Sanskrit it's yana, something that carries you. Buddhist texts speak of more than one vehicle toward awakening. Tibetan teachers describe three, and the point they make is that one person can ride all three at once. Second, the foundation: renunciation. The first vehicle, as Tibetans frame it, is about seeing clearly that grasping brings suffering, and turning away from it. Ethics, simplicity, the vows of personal liberation, the four thoughts that turn the mind from year one. A word of care here: this layer has sometimes been given a name that sounds like lesser, and Theravada Buddhists, who follow the way of the elders, describe their own path in their own terms and don't use that name for themselves. In the Tibetan scheme, the first vehicle names a layer inside every practitioner, not someone else's school. Third, the great vehicle: compassion. On top of renunciation sits bodhicitta, the wish to wake up not for yourself alone but for all beings, and the wisdom that sees things as empty of a fixed self. Tonglen and mind training live here. Fourth, the diamond vehicle. On top of both sit the methods of tantra: mantra, visualization, the bond with a teacher. Tibetan teachers say this top floor stands on the lower ones, and without them it falls. That's why a monk can keep the vows of a monk, the vows of a bodhisattva, and the commitments of tantra all at the same time. Renunciation, compassion, and the diamond path: in this telling, they are one path walked on three levels.
screen: `YANA: SOMETHING THAT CARRIES YOU.` · `THE FOUNDATION: RENUNCIATION.` · `THE GREAT VEHICLE: COMPASSION.` · `THE DIAMOND PATH, ON TOP OF BOTH.` · then, large: `ALL THREE AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Name the three, one at a time, slowly, with a breath for each. First: renunciation. Notice one thing you're holding too tightly, and loosen your grip a little. Second: compassion. Bring to mind one person, and wish them well. Third: the diamond path. Let a sound, a mantra if you have one or just a quiet hum, rest in your chest. Then hold all three together, as one breath. The bell holds the time.
Three vehicles. In Tibetan teaching, renunciation, compassion and the diamond path, practiced together as layers of one path, each standing on the one below. Today's word.
Your line: all three at once. Today, in one moment, let go of something small, wish someone well, and give it your full attention. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists describe practicing three vehicles together, renunciation and ethics, the compassion of the bodhisattva, and the methods of tantra, and monastics may keep the vows of all three at once.

myth: in Tibetan teaching, you pick one vehicle and drop the others
Tibetan teachers describe practicing all three together, as layers.
the diamond vehicle stands on the lower two
Tibetan teachers say without renunciation and compassion it falls.
Theravada Buddhists call their own path by the Tibetan name for the first vehicle
they describe their own path in their own terms, as the way of the elders.

fork.setup: a Tibetan monk has taken a monk's vows, a bodhisattva's vows and the commitments of tantra. which does he keep today?
options: only the highest, the tantric ones.
fork.reveal: in the Tibetan telling they're layers of one path, so a monk keeps all three at the same time.

original.note: Sanskrit: yana, a vehicle, something that carries you. it's the yana in Mahayana and Vajrayana.

trapdoor: what you thought: three vehicles means three rival kinds of Buddhism.
what it means: in Tibetan teaching, three layers of one path, renunciation, compassion, the diamond path, practiced at once.
what a scholar hears: a monk keeping the vows of personal liberation, the bodhisattva vows and tantric commitments together.

notes: The script deliberately avoids the term 'Hinayana' and explains why; a Keeper should check that the paragraph is fair to Theravada Buddhists and to Tibetan usage.
Three sets of vows (pratimoksha, bodhisattva, tantric) kept together by one practitioner: confirm framing.
'Buddhist texts speak of more than one vehicle' is general (e.g. the Lotus Sutra); confirm.
The 'four thoughts that turn the mind' recalls year one, day 308.
